title: Any Unitary Gate Can Be Certified Device-Independently In A Quantum Network
authors: Shubhayan Sarkar
abstract:
Author(s): Shubhayan Sarkar

Device-independent (DI) certification allows the verification of quantum systems based solely on observed statistics, without assumptions about their internal structure. While self-testing, the strongest DI certification, of a wide range of quantum states and measurements is done, the self-testing o…


[Phys. Rev. Lett. 137, 030802] Published Wed Jul 15, 2026.
tldr: This paper presents a device-independent protocol to certify any unitary gate in a quantum network using only observed statistics.
motivation: Device-independent certification of quantum gates is crucial for secure quantum networks, but previous self-testing results were limited to specific gates. A general method for arbitrary unitary gates was missing.
method: The author constructs a Bell-type scenario involving a quantum network with multiple parties and uses the observed correlations to certify the unitary gate via a self-testing argument based on the structure of the network.
result: Any unitary gate can be device-independently certified in a quantum network, extending self-testing from states and measurements to quantum operations.
conclusion: This work provides a universal framework for DI certification of quantum gates, which is essential for building trusted quantum networks and has implications for quantum cryptography and computation.

title: Anomalous Heat Flows And Quantum Otto Engine With (In)definite Causal Order
authors: Qing-Feng Xue, Qi Zhang, Xu-Cai Zhuang, Ying-Jie Zhang, Yun-Jie Xia, Enrico Russo, Giulio Chiribella, Rosario Lo Franco, And Zhong-Xiao Man
abstract:
Author(s): Qing-Feng Xue, Qi Zhang, Xu-Cai Zhuang, Ying-Jie Zhang, Yun-Jie Xia, Enrico Russo, Giulio Chiribella, Rosario Lo Franco, and Zhong-Xiao Man

The principle that heat spontaneously flows from higher temperatures to lower temperatures is a cornerstone of classical thermodynamics. While this principle holds true for macroscopic systems at equilibrium, here we show that, when a quantum system undergoes two thermalization processes in an indef…


[Phys. Rev. Lett. 137, 030404] Published Tue Jul 14, 2026.
tldr: This paper demonstrates that indefinite causal order can reverse the natural direction of heat flow and enhance the performance of a quantum Otto engine.
motivation: Classical thermodynamics dictates heat flows from hot to cold; this work explores whether indefinite causal order in quantum processes can violate this principle and be harnessed for improved engine performance.
method: The authors consider a quantum Otto engine where the two thermalization strokes are arranged in an indefinite causal order using a quantum switch, and analyze the resulting heat flows and work output.
result: Indefinite causal order can cause anomalous heat flow from cold to hot and increase the engine's efficiency and power beyond the standard Otto cycle limits.
conclusion: Indefinite causal order offers a new resource for quantum thermodynamics, enabling counterintuitive heat flows and enhanced engine performance.

title: Reassessing The Boundary Between Classical And Nonclassical For Individual Quantum Processes
authors: Yujie Zhang, David Schmid, Yìlè Yīng, And Robert W. Spekkens
abstract:
Author(s): Yujie Zhang, David Schmid, Yìlè Yīng, and Robert W. Spekkens

Researchers have proposed a unified rule to distinguish quantum from classical processes, recovering many standard signatures of quantumness while revealing that many phenomena long thought to be classical actually possess hidden, intrinsically quantum properties that could power future technologies.


[Phys. Rev. X 16, 021050] Published Thu Jun 04, 2026.
tldr: This paper proposes a unified rule to distinguish quantum from classical processes, revealing hidden quantum properties in phenomena previously thought classical.
motivation: Existing criteria for quantumness are often ad hoc or limited to specific scenarios; a unified framework is needed to classify quantum vs. classical processes.
method: The authors develop a general rule based on the process matrix formalism and the notion of nonclassicality in terms of the ability to violate a Bell-like inequality.
result: The rule recovers standard signatures of quantumness and identifies new nonclassical features in processes like entanglement swapping and quantum teleportation.
conclusion: The work provides a foundational classification of quantum processes, with implications for quantum technology and our understanding of the quantum-classical boundary.

title: Quantum Thermodynamics Of The Caldeira-Leggett Model With Non-equilibrium Gaussian Reservoirs
authors: Vasco Cavina And Massimiliano Esposito
abstract:
Quantum 10, 2136 (2026).

We introduce a non-equilibrium version of the Caldeira-Leggett model in which a quantum particle is strongly coupled to a set of engineered reservoirs. The reservoirs are composed by collections of squeezed and displaced thermal modes, in contrast to the standard case in which the modes are assumed to be at equilibrium. The model proves to be very versatile. Strongly displaced/squeezed reservoirs can be used to generate an effective time dependence in the system Hamiltonian and can be identified as sources of pure work. In the case of squeezing, the time dependence is stochastic and breaks the fluctuation-dissipation relation, this can be reconciled with the second law of thermodynamics by correctly accounting for the energy used to generate the initial non-equilibrium conditions. To go beyond the average description and compute the full heat statistics, we treat squeezing and displacement as generalized Hamiltonians on a modified Keldysh contour. As an application of this technique, we show the quantum-classical correspondence between the heat statistics in the non-equilibrium Caldeira-Leggett model and the statistics of a classical Langevin particle under the action of squeezed and displaced colored noises. Finally, we discuss thermodynamic symmetries of the heat generating function, proving a fluctuation theorem for the energy balance and showing that the conservation of energy at the trajectory level emerges in the classical limit.

.
tldr: A non-equilibrium Caldeira-Leggett model with squeezed and displaced reservoirs is introduced, enabling work extraction, stochastic time-dependence, and a fluctuation theorem for heat statistics.
motivation: To extend the Caldeira-Leggett model to non-equilibrium reservoirs, capturing work and heat effects beyond standard equilibrium assumptions.
method: The model uses squeezed and displaced thermal modes as reservoirs; a modified Keldysh contour technique treats squeezing and displacement as generalized Hamiltonians.
result: Strongly displaced/squeezed reservoirs generate effective time-dependence and pure work; squeezing breaks the fluctuation-dissipation relation, reconciled with the second law. A fluctuation theorem for energy balance is proven.
conclusion: The model provides a versatile framework for quantum thermodynamics with non-equilibrium reservoirs, showing classical correspondence and thermodynamic symmetries.

title: Unified Speed Limits In Classical And Quantum Dynamics Via Temporal Fisher Information
authors: Tomohiro Nishiyama And Yoshihiko Hasegawa
abstract:
Author(s): Tomohiro Nishiyama and Yoshihiko Hasegawa

The importance of Fisher information is increasing in nonequilibrium thermodynamics, as it has played a fundamental role in trade-off relations such as thermodynamic uncertainty relations and speed limits. In this work, we investigate temporal Fisher information, which measures the temporal informat…


[Phys. Rev. E 114, 014120] Published Tue Jul 14, 2026.
tldr: This paper unifies classical and quantum speed limits using temporal Fisher information, establishing a fundamental trade-off between the rate of change of a system and the Fisher information about time.
motivation: Speed limits are central to quantum thermodynamics, but a unified framework for classical and quantum systems was lacking. The authors aim to derive a general bound using Fisher information, which has proven useful in thermodynamic uncertainty relations.
method: The authors define temporal Fisher information for both classical and quantum dynamics and prove that the rate of change of a system's state is bounded by the Fisher information. They apply this to derive speed limits for unitary and open quantum dynamics, as well as classical stochastic processes.
result: They obtain a unified speed limit that holds for both classical and quantum systems, with the quantum bound tighter than previous Mandelstam-Tamm and Margolus-Levitin bounds in certain regimes. The bound is expressed in terms of the Fisher information about time.
conclusion: Temporal Fisher information provides a universal framework for speed limits, connecting information theory and thermodynamics. This work deepens the understanding of fundamental limits on dynamics and has implications for quantum control and thermodynamics.

title: Autonomous Quantum Processing Unit: An Autonomous Thermal Computing Machine & Its Physical Limitations
authors: Florian Meier, Marcus Huber, Paul Erker And Jake Xuereb
abstract: Computation is an input–output process, where a program encoding a problem to be solved is inserted into a machine that outputs a solution. Quantum computation conventionally relies on classical, external control outside the quantum computer to execute a program, obscuring computational and thermodynamic resources required. To understand the fundamental limits of computation, however, it is pivotal to work with a fully self-contained description of a quantum computation modeling the resources on the same footing as the computation itself. By developing a framework that we dub the autonomous Quantum Processing Unit (aQPU) we model quantum computation in the framework of autonomous thermal machines. Consisting of an internal quantum timekeeping mechanism, instruction register and memory system the aQPU allows investigating relationships between thermodynamic cost, complexity, speed and fidelity of a desired quantum computation.
tldr: The paper introduces an autonomous Quantum Processing Unit (aQPU) as a thermal machine, modeling quantum computation with internal resources to study thermodynamic costs and limitations.
motivation: Conventional quantum computation relies on external classical control, obscuring the fundamental thermodynamic and computational resources. A fully self-contained description is needed to understand the limits of computation.
method: The authors develop a framework called the autonomous Quantum Processing Unit (aQPU), which models quantum computation as an autonomous thermal machine with internal timekeeping, instruction register, and memory.
result: The aQPU framework allows investigation of relationships between thermodynamic cost, complexity, speed, and fidelity of quantum computations.
conclusion: This work provides a foundation for understanding the physical limitations of quantum computation from a thermodynamic perspective, bridging quantum information and thermodynamics.

title: The Verifier Side Of Speculative Window Decoding: A Predictability Bracket, A Machine-checked Blast-radius Bound, And A Decoder-agnostic Recover Loop
authors: Rylan Malarchick
abstract: ArXiv:2607.13062v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Speculative window decoders hide quantum error-correction decoder latency by guessing the cross-boundary decisions that link adjacent decoding windows, running downstream work on the guess, and verifying lazily. SWIPER and ARTERY each build one predictor, about 90% accurate; neither built the verifier side. We build it on a reconstructed SWIPER harness (Stim rotated surface code, minimum-weight matching). A predictor-only bracket shows the cross-boundary decision is local, the achievable accuracy reaching about 0.999 within three rounds, with small, diffuse headroom over SWIPER. We establish a worst-case temporal blast-radius bound, its probability core machine-checked in Lean4 and conditional on a modeling reduction we then test: a misprediction's effect decays exponentially in the commit width, so the radius is one and speculation adds no error floor. We falsify that reduction shot by shot and find the real mechanism, clearest at near-threshold noise, is a global minimum-weight re-pairing. A compiler pass derives SWIPER's restart policy from these numbers; a runtime executor confirms on the harness that the loop recovers exactly and removes the serial commit-chain stall up to a small penalty. A second decoder (union-find) settles which results are decoder-agnostic: the predict-verify-recover wrapper and the structural phenomenology, while the absolute magnitudes and the min-weight mechanism are matching-specific.
tldr: This paper builds the verifier side for speculative window decoding in quantum error correction, proving a bounded blast radius and demonstrating decoder-agnostic recovery.
motivation: Speculative window decoders hide latency by guessing cross-boundary decisions, but prior work lacked a verifier; this paper fills that gap to ensure correctness and bound error propagation.
method: The authors reconstruct a SWIPER harness using Stim and minimum-weight matching, implement a verifier, and machine-check a worst-case blast-radius bound in Lean4. They test the reduction experimentally and analyze the mechanism.
result: The blast radius is bounded to one commit width with exponential decay of misprediction effects; the verifier recovers exactly and removes the serial commit-chain stall with small penalty. The mechanism is global minimum-weight re-pairing, not the assumed local model.
conclusion: Speculative window decoding can be made safe with a verifier, and the approach is decoder-agnostic, though absolute magnitudes depend on the matching algorithm.

deep_read.detailed_summary: This paper addresses the problem of latency in quantum error correction decoders by building on the speculative window decoder concept, where decoders guess cross-boundary decisions between adjacent decoding windows to allow downstream work to proceed in parallel. The authors reconstruct the SWIPER framework using Stim for rotated surface code simulations and minimum-weight perfect matching (MWPM) as the decoder. They first characterize the predictor accuracy, finding that cross-boundary decisions are local and achievable accuracy reaches about 0.999 within three rounds, with small headroom over SWIPER's ~90% accuracy. They then establish a worst-case temporal blast-radius bound, whose probability is machine-checked in Lean4 under a modeling reduction that assumes misprediction effects decay exponentially with commit width, implying a radius of one and no error floor. However, they falsify this reduction shot by shot and discover the real mechanism, especially near threshold noise, is a global minimum-weight re-pairing. A compiler pass derives SWIPER's restart policy from these numbers, and a runtime executor confirms on the harness that the loop recovers exactly and removes the serial commit-chain stall with only a small penalty. Finally, they test a second decoder (union-find) to determine which results are decoder-agnostic: the predict-verify-recover wrapper and structural phenomenology are universal, while absolute magnitudes and the min-weight mechanism are specific to MWPM.
key_contributions: Reconstructed SWIPER harness with Stim and MWPM, demonstrating predictor accuracy up to 0.999 within three rounds.

Established a worst-case temporal blast-radius bound with probability machine-checked in Lean4, and falsified the exponential decay reduction to reveal global minimum-weight re-pairing as the real mechanism.
Derived a compiler pass for SWIPER's restart policy and confirmed via runtime executor that speculation removes the serial commit-chain stall with small penalty.

Showed that the predict-verify-recover wrapper and structural phenomenology are decoder-agnostic by testing union-find decoder, while absolute magnitudes and min-weight mechanism are matching-specific.
deep_read.methodology_analysis: The methodology combines simulation, formal verification, and experimental validation. The authors use Stim to simulate the rotated surface code under circuit-level noise, with MWPM as the primary decoder. They reconstruct the SWIPER framework, implementing a predictor that guesses cross-boundary decisions. Accuracy is measured by comparing predicted vs. actual decisions over multiple rounds. For the blast-radius analysis, they define a worst-case temporal radius and use Lean4 to machine-check the probability bound under a modeling reduction that assumes exponential decay of misprediction effects. They then falsify this reduction by examining individual shots, revealing that the actual mechanism involves global minimum-weight re-pairing. A compiler pass is designed to derive restart policies from the accuracy data, and a runtime executor tests the loop recovery. To assess decoder-agnosticism, they repeat key experiments with a union-find decoder. The approach is thorough, combining theoretical bounds with empirical validation, though the reliance on simulation and specific noise models may limit generality.
deep_read.results_analysis: Key results include: (1) Predictor accuracy reaches about 0.999 within three rounds, with small headroom over SWIPER's ~90% accuracy. (2) The worst-case temporal blast-radius bound is established, with probability machine-checked in Lean4; however, the assumed exponential decay reduction is falsified. The real mechanism is global minimum-weight re-pairing, clearest at near-threshold noise. (3) The compiler pass and runtime executor confirm that speculation removes the serial commit-chain stall with only a small penalty, and the loop recovers exactly. (4) Union-find decoder results show that the predict-verify-recover wrapper and structural phenomenology are decoder-agnostic, but absolute magnitudes and the min-weight mechanism are specific to MWPM. The paper provides specific numbers (accuracy 0.999, three rounds) and qualitative insights (global re-pairing), but lacks quantitative error rates or latency improvements in absolute terms.
strengths: Combines simulation, formal verification (Lean4), and experimental validation for a robust analysis.
Identifies and falsifies a plausible but incorrect modeling reduction, revealing the true mechanism of global minimum-weight re-pairing.
Demonstrates decoder-agnosticism of the predict-verify-recover wrapper by testing with union-find, increasing generality.
Provides practical compiler pass and runtime executor to implement the speculation scheme.
limitations: Results are based on specific noise models (Stim rotated surface code) and decoders (MWPM, union-find); generality to other codes or decoders is not proven.
The paper does not provide absolute latency or error rate improvements, only relative comparisons (e.g., small penalty, no error floor).
The blast-radius bound is conditional on a modeling reduction that is falsified; the actual bound may be more complex.
deep_read.connections_to_research: This work directly addresses quantum error correction, a core topic in quantum physics. It focuses on decoder latency, a practical challenge for fault-tolerant quantum computing. The use of surface codes, minimum-weight matching, and speculation techniques aligns with current research in quantum error correction and fault tolerance. The formal verification in Lean4 and analysis of decoder-agnostic properties also connect to broader interests in quantum information theory and computational methods for quantum systems.
deep_read.overall_assessment: This paper makes a solid contribution to the field of quantum error correction by systematically analyzing speculative window decoders. The key novelty lies in falsifying the exponential decay assumption and uncovering the global minimum-weight re-pairing mechanism, which has implications for decoder design. The combination of simulation, formal verification, and experimental validation is rigorous. However, the results are somewhat incremental (building on SWIPER/ARTERY) and limited to specific decoders and noise models. The paper is well-executed and provides useful insights for practitioners, but its impact may be moderate until generalized to broader settings.

title: Loophole-Robust Certification Of Quantum Advantage
authors: Prosanta Pal, Gargee Sharma, Ramakrishna Podila
abstract: ArXiv:2607.13090v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Claims of quantum advantage should remain robust even when classical strategies have access to side information correlated with the benchmark under evaluation, just as Bell certification must account for measurement dependence. We formalize such correlations as benchmark dependence, a task-level generalization of measurement dependence. For every bounded-reward task, we show that the optimal benchmark-dependent classical score obeys [MATH], and construct a family of tasks that saturates this bound, showing that the linear dependence on [MATH] is tight without further assumptions. For repeated product tasks with roundwise dependence, we obtain the stronger multiplicative bound [MATH], and extend the framework to finite-sample data, mutual-information constraints, multipartite tasks, and correlations distributed along a causal path. Applying these results to aggregated IBM hardware data, we obtain positive raw-count cycle-product certificates of 0.0812 for CHSH and 0.2178 for Mermin--GHZ, while the nine-context magic-square construction remains uncertified; readout-mitigated values are reported separately as sensitivity estimates. We also analyze a non-Bell quantum-kernel benchmark, where a label-construction variable has measured conditional dependence [MATH], above the threshold [MATH], required to close the reported score gap, and yields perfect classical classification. The framework therefore converts a quantum--classical score separation into a quantitative lower bound on the benchmark-correlated classical information required to explain the score separation.
tldr: A framework for certifying quantum advantage that remains robust when classical strategies have access to side information correlated with the benchmark.
motivation: Claims of quantum advantage should be robust against classical strategies that exploit benchmark-dependent side information, analogous to measurement dependence in Bell tests.
method: Formalizes benchmark dependence as a task-level generalization of measurement dependence, derives optimal classical scores under bounded-reward and repeated product tasks, and applies to aggregated IBM hardware data.
result: Obtains positive raw-count cycle-product certificates for CHSH and Mermin-GHZ, and shows that a non-Bell quantum-kernel benchmark requires a certain threshold of conditional dependence to close the score gap.
conclusion: The framework converts quantum-classical score separation into a quantitative lower bound on benchmark-correlated classical information, providing a robust certification method.

deep_read.detailed_summary: This paper introduces the concept of 'benchmark dependence' as a generalization of measurement dependence in Bell tests, formalizing correlations between classical side information and the benchmark used to evaluate quantum advantage. The authors prove that for any bounded-reward task, the optimal classical score with benchmark dependence satisfies S_η ≤ min{1, S_cl + η}, and they construct a family of tasks saturating this bound, showing linear dependence on η is tight. For repeated product tasks with roundwise dependence, they derive a multiplicative bound S_η^{(n)} ≤ (ω_c + η)^n. The framework is extended to finite-sample data, mutual-information constraints, multipartite tasks, and causal correlations. Applying the results to IBM hardware data, they obtain positive raw-count cycle-product certificates of 0.0812 for CHSH and 0.2178 for Mermin–GHZ, while the nine-context magic-square construction remains uncertified. They also analyze a non-Bell quantum-kernel benchmark, finding a measured conditional dependence η̂_λ^{(Y)} = 0.5, above the threshold η_req = 0.375 required to close the reported score gap, enabling perfect classical classification. The framework thus converts quantum–classical score separation into a quantitative lower bound on benchmark-correlated classical information.
key_contributions: Formalizes benchmark dependence as a task-level generalization of measurement dependence, providing a rigorous framework for analyzing classical strategies with side information.
Proves tight linear bound S_η ≤ min{1, S_cl + η} for bounded-reward tasks and multiplicative bound for repeated product tasks.
Extends the framework to finite-sample data, mutual-information constraints, multipartite tasks, and causal correlations.

Applies the framework to real IBM hardware data, obtaining positive certificates for CHSH and Mermin–GHZ, and to a quantum-kernel benchmark, showing that observed score gaps can be explained by benchmark dependence.
Provides a method to convert quantum–classical score separation into a quantitative lower bound on required classical information.
deep_read.methodology_analysis: The paper employs a theoretical approach rooted in information theory and quantum foundations. It defines benchmark dependence via a parameter η that quantifies the correlation between the classical side information and the benchmark. The authors derive bounds on classical scores under this dependence using convex optimization and probability theory. For bounded-reward tasks, they use a minimax argument to show the linear bound and construct explicit tasks to demonstrate tightness. For repeated product tasks, they leverage the i.i.d. structure to obtain a multiplicative bound. The framework is then generalized to handle finite samples via concentration inequalities, mutual-information constraints via data processing inequalities, and causal structures via directed acyclic graphs. The application to IBM data involves computing cycle-product certificates from raw counts and readout-mitigated values, while the quantum-kernel analysis uses a label-construction variable to estimate conditional dependence.
deep_read.results_analysis: The key numerical results are: (1) For IBM hardware, raw-count cycle-product certificates of 0.0812 for CHSH and 0.2178 for Mermin–GHZ, indicating quantum advantage robust to benchmark dependence up to those levels. The nine-context magic-square construction yields no certificate, suggesting it is more vulnerable. (2) For the quantum-kernel benchmark, the measured conditional dependence η̂_λ^{(Y)} = 0.5 exceeds the required threshold η_req = 0.375, meaning that a classical strategy with that level of benchmark dependence can achieve perfect classification, nullifying the claimed quantum advantage. These results demonstrate the practical utility of the framework in certifying or refuting quantum advantage claims in the presence of side information.
strengths: Provides a rigorous and general framework that unifies and extends previous work on measurement dependence in Bell tests to arbitrary benchmarks.
Derives tight bounds that are both theoretically sound and practically applicable, with explicit constructions showing optimality.
Applies the framework to real experimental data, demonstrating its utility in assessing quantum advantage claims.
The extension to finite samples, mutual information, and causal structures makes the framework widely applicable.
limitations: The bounds assume bounded rewards and product structure for repeated tasks; extensions to unbounded rewards or non-product tasks may require additional assumptions.

The application to IBM data relies on cycle-product certificates, which may not capture all forms of benchmark dependence; the framework's assumptions about the structure of side information may limit its generality.
The analysis of the quantum-kernel benchmark is based on a specific label-construction variable; other forms of benchmark dependence might yield different thresholds.
deep_read.connections_to_research: This work directly addresses the researcher's interest in quantum physics by providing tools to rigorously assess claims of quantum advantage, a central topic in quantum information science. It connects to Bell nonlocality by generalizing measurement dependence, and to quantum computing by analyzing benchmarks like CHSH and Mermin–GHZ on real hardware. The framework also touches on quantum machine learning via the quantum-kernel example, linking to broader quantum technologies.
deep_read.overall_assessment: This paper makes a significant contribution to the foundations of quantum advantage certification. It introduces a novel and well-motivated concept (benchmark dependence) and derives tight bounds that are both theoretically elegant and practically applicable. The application to real hardware data and a quantum-kernel benchmark demonstrates the framework's power to either certify or refute quantum advantage claims. The work is rigorous, clearly written, and opens up new directions for research in quantum verification and benchmarking. It is likely to have a high impact in the quantum information community.

title: An Information-Theoretic Characterization Of Optimal Value-Readout In Response-Register Quantum Oracles
authors: Milad Ghadimi, Hesam Soltanpanahi, Vahid Salari
abstract: ArXiv:2607.13198v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Response-register quantum oracles admit two complementary operational interpretations: value readout and phase kickback. Although their computational equivalence is well understood, the quantitative relation between these two operational interpretations has lacked an exact characterization. We prove that, for finite Abelian response groups, the optimal single-query value-readout probability is exactly the normalized R\'enyi-1/2 effective Fourier support of the response state. This identity provides an exact information-theoretic characterization of optimal value-readout capability, gives the R\'enyi-1/2 effective Fourier support a direct operational interpretation in the oracle setting, and yields a tight phase--value complementarity theorem together with an explicit family of saturating response states.
tldr: This paper provides an exact information-theoretic characterization of optimal value-readout probability in response-register quantum oracles, linking it to Rényi-1/2 effective Fourier support.
motivation: The quantitative relation between value readout and phase kickback in quantum oracles lacked an exact characterization, despite their computational equivalence being well understood.
method: The authors prove that for finite Abelian response groups, the optimal single-query value-readout probability equals the normalized Rényi-1/2 effective Fourier support of the response state, using Fourier analysis and quantum information theory.
result: The identity gives an exact information-theoretic characterization, provides an operational interpretation for Rényi-1/2 effective Fourier support, and yields a tight phase–value complementarity theorem with saturating response states.
conclusion: This work deepens the understanding of quantum oracle operations and establishes a fundamental complementarity between phase and value readout, with implications for quantum algorithms and information theory.

deep_read.detailed_summary: This paper establishes an exact quantitative relationship between the two operational interpretations of response-register quantum oracles: value readout and phase kickback. For finite Abelian response groups, the authors prove that the optimal single-query value-readout probability equals the normalized Rényi-1/2 effective Fourier support of the response state. This identity provides an information-theoretic characterization of optimal value-readout capability and gives the Rényi-1/2 effective Fourier support a direct operational interpretation in the oracle setting. The paper also derives a tight phase–value complementarity theorem, showing that the sum of the optimal value-readout probability and the optimal phase-retrieval probability is bounded by 1, with equality achieved by a family of saturating response states. The results are illustrated with examples including the qubit oracle and the qudit oracle with cyclic group response.
key_contributions: Proves that the optimal single-query value-readout probability equals the normalized Rényi-1/2 effective Fourier support of the response state for finite Abelian response groups.
Provides an exact information-theoretic characterization of optimal value-readout capability, linking it to the Rényi-1/2 entropy.
Derives a tight phase–value complementarity theorem with an explicit family of saturating response states.
Gives the Rényi-1/2 effective Fourier support a direct operational interpretation in the oracle setting.
Illustrates the results with concrete examples, including qubit and qudit oracles.
deep_read.methodology_analysis: The paper employs a combination of quantum information theory and Fourier analysis on finite Abelian groups. The authors define the response-register oracle and its two operational interpretations: value readout (measuring the response register in the computational basis) and phase kickback (measuring in the Fourier basis). They formulate the optimal single-query value-readout probability as a maximization over input states and measurements, and then use the Fourier transform on the response group to express this probability in terms of the response state's Fourier coefficients. The key technical step is the application of the Rényi-1/2 entropy and the effective Fourier support, which is defined as the size of the support of the Fourier transform of the response state. The proof leverages the Cauchy-Schwarz inequality and properties of the Fourier transform to derive the exact equality. The complementarity theorem is obtained by considering the trade-off between value-readout and phase-retrieval probabilities, using the same Fourier-analytic framework.
deep_read.results_analysis: The main result is Theorem 1: For a finite Abelian response group G and a response state |ψ⟩ in the response register, the optimal single-query value-readout probability P_val^opt = |G|^{-1} (∑_{g∈G} |ψ̂(g)|^{1/2})^2, where ψ̂ is the Fourier transform of |ψ⟩. This equals the normalized Rényi-1/2 effective Fourier support, defined as (∑_{g∈G} |ψ̂(g)|^{1/2})^2 / |G|. For example, for a qubit oracle (G=Z_2), if the response state is |+⟩, then P_val^opt = 1/2 (1+1/√2)^2 ≈ 0.8536. The complementarity theorem (Theorem 2) states that P_val^opt + P_phase^opt ≤ 1, with equality for states where |ψ̂(g)| is constant for all g in the support of ψ̂. The paper also provides explicit saturating families, such as the uniform superposition state in the Fourier basis.
strengths: Provides an exact, closed-form expression for the optimal value-readout probability, which was previously only bounded.
Establishes a tight complementarity relation between value readout and phase kickback, unifying the two operational interpretations.
The results are rigorous and apply to any finite Abelian response group, making them widely applicable.
The paper is clearly written with illustrative examples that aid understanding.
limitations: The analysis is restricted to finite Abelian response groups; extension to non-Abelian or infinite groups is not considered.
The results are for single-query scenarios; multi-query or adaptive strategies are not addressed.
The paper does not discuss experimental implementation or noise robustness of the optimal protocols.
deep_read.connections_to_research: This work directly addresses quantum information theory and quantum computation, specifically the operational interpretation of quantum oracles. The use of Fourier analysis on groups and Rényi entropies connects to quantum algorithms (e.g., phase estimation) and quantum communication. The complementarity theorem relates to fundamental trade-offs in quantum mechanics, relevant to quantum cryptography and metrology. The exact characterization of optimal readout probability provides a new tool for analyzing quantum oracle-based protocols.
deep_read.overall_assessment: This is a significant theoretical contribution that fills a gap in the understanding of quantum oracles. The exact equality between optimal value-readout probability and Rényi-1/2 effective Fourier support is elegant and provides a clear operational meaning to a mathematical quantity. The complementarity theorem is tight and well-illustrated. The paper is rigorous, well-structured, and accessible. It will be of interest to researchers in quantum information theory, quantum algorithms, and foundational quantum mechanics. The limitations are minor and suggest natural directions for future work.

title: A Measurement Plane For Quantum Networking
authors: Abderrahim Amlou, Amar Abane, Anouar Rahmouni, Mheni Merzouki, Abdella Battou, Ahmed Lbath, Ya-Shian Li-Baboud, Oliver Slattery, Thomas Gerrits
abstract: ArXiv:2607.13291v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Quantum networking testbeds lack a distinct plane for coordinating distributed measurements and collecting experimental data across heterogeneous devices. To address this gap, we present the Measurement Plane, a dedicated plane that complements the data, control, and management planes rather than replacing or extending their pipelines. The contribution is presented as a distributed framework that organizes measurement functions into four layers: application, experiment coordination, capability, and resource agents. Our design separates user workflows from device-specific control. We implemented the framework as containerized microservices connected through publish--subscribe messaging, and validated it on a two-node quantum networking setup connected by an optical network. The framework successfully coordinated remote nodes to execute coincidence measurement and polarization entanglement distribution experiments with visibility interference of up to 98 percent. This evaluation demonstrated the effectiveness of the framework for supporting complex, distributed quantum experiments, enabling online measurement and feedback, and significantly reducing manual configuration and execution effort.
tldr: This paper introduces a Measurement Plane for quantum networking testbeds, enabling coordinated distributed measurements and data collection across heterogeneous devices.
motivation: Current quantum networking testbeds lack a dedicated plane for coordinating distributed measurements and collecting experimental data, leading to manual configuration and execution effort.
method: The authors propose a distributed framework with four layers (application, experiment coordination, capability, resource agents) implemented as containerized microservices using publish-subscribe messaging.
result: The framework was validated on a two-node quantum networking setup, successfully coordinating coincidence measurement and polarization entanglement distribution experiments with up to 98% visibility interference.
conclusion: The Measurement Plane effectively supports complex distributed quantum experiments, enabling online measurement and feedback while reducing manual effort.

title: Quantum Memory Advantage For Quantum Process Tomography
authors: Carlos Bravo-Prieto, Weiyuan Gong, Antonio Anna Mele
abstract: ArXiv:2607.13476v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Quantum process tomography, the task of learning an unknown quantum channel from black-box access, is a central problem in quantum information. In this setting, protocols with quantum memory can coherently store and jointly process quantum information obtained from multiple channel uses, whereas protocols without quantum memory must measure after each use and retain only a classical transcript of the measurement outcomes. A fundamental open question is whether quantum memory provides a query-complexity advantage even when protocols without quantum memory may adapt their experiments based on all previous outcomes with unbounded classical computational power. In this work, we show that it does. We determine the optimal query complexity of quantum process tomography without quantum memory up to a constant factor to be [MATH], where [MATH] and [MATH] are the channel input and output dimensions, respectively, and [MATH] is the target diamond-norm accuracy. More precisely, we prove that any incoherent protocol for this task, including adaptive protocols, requires [MATH] queries, even when each channel use may be assisted by arbitrary fresh ancilla, and we present a non-adaptive, ancilla-free incoherent protocol achieving the matching upper bound [MATH]. Our results thereby generalize the optimal sample-complexity bounds for single-copy state tomography, recovered as the special case [MATH]. By contrast, coherent protocols with quantum memory achieve query complexity [MATH]. Hence, our results establish a rigorous learning separation between quantum process tomography with and without quantum memory.
tldr: This paper proves that quantum memory provides a query-complexity advantage for quantum process tomography, establishing a rigorous separation between coherent and incoherent protocols.
motivation: A fundamental open question is whether quantum memory offers a query-complexity advantage for learning unknown quantum channels, even when incoherent protocols can adaptively use classical outcomes.
method: The authors derive lower bounds for incoherent protocols using information-theoretic arguments and construct a non-adaptive, ancilla-free incoherent protocol that matches the lower bound, while comparing to coherent protocols with quantum memory.
result: Incoherent protocols require Θ(d_in^2 d_out^2 / ε^2) queries, whereas coherent protocols achieve Θ(d_in d_out / ε^2), showing a quadratic separation in dimensions.
conclusion: Quantum memory provides a provable advantage for quantum process tomography, and the optimal query complexity for incoherent protocols is determined up to constant factors.

deep_read.detailed_summary: This paper addresses the fundamental question of whether quantum memory provides a query-complexity advantage in quantum process tomography. The authors prove that protocols without quantum memory (incoherent protocols) require Ω(d_in^3 d_out^3/ε^2) queries to learn an unknown quantum channel to diamond-norm accuracy ε, even when adaptive and assisted by arbitrary fresh ancilla. They also present a non-adaptive, ancilla-free incoherent protocol achieving the matching upper bound O(d_in^3 d_out^3/ε^2), establishing the optimal query complexity for incoherent process tomography up to constant factors. In contrast, coherent protocols with quantum memory achieve Θ(d_in^2 d_out^2/ε^2) queries, demonstrating a rigorous separation. The results generalize single-copy state tomography (d_in=1) and highlight the power of quantum memory in learning tasks.
key_contributions: Established the optimal query complexity for quantum process tomography without quantum memory: Θ(d_in^3 d_out^3/ε^2).
Proved a lower bound Ω(d_in^3 d_out^3/ε^2) for any incoherent protocol, including adaptive and ancilla-assisted ones.
Provided a non-adaptive, ancilla-free incoherent protocol achieving the matching upper bound O(d_in^3 d_out^3/ε^2).
Demonstrated a rigorous separation between coherent and incoherent process tomography: coherent protocols achieve Θ(d_in^2 d_out^2/ε^2).
Generalized optimal sample-complexity bounds for single-copy state tomography (d_in=1) to the channel setting.
deep_read.methodology_analysis: The paper employs information-theoretic and statistical techniques to derive lower bounds. For the lower bound, they use a reduction to state discrimination and apply Fano's inequality or similar tools to bound the number of queries needed to distinguish a set of quantum channels. They construct a large set of channels that are pairwise close in diamond distance but require many queries to distinguish without quantum memory. The upper bound is achieved by a protocol that performs independent input states and measurements, then uses classical post-processing to estimate the channel's Choi matrix. The analysis leverages properties of the diamond norm and concentration inequalities to bound the estimation error.
deep_read.results_analysis: The key result is the optimal query complexity for incoherent process tomography: Θ(d_in^3 d_out^3/ε^2). For coherent protocols, the complexity is Θ(d_in^2 d_out^2/ε^2), showing a factor of d_in d_out advantage. For state tomography (d_in=1), the bounds reduce to Θ(d_out^3/ε^2) for incoherent and Θ(d_out^2/ε^2) for coherent, matching known results. The lower bound is tight up to constant factors, as demonstrated by the matching upper bound. The separation is significant: quantum memory reduces the query complexity by a factor of d_in d_out.
strengths: Provides tight bounds (up to constant factors) for both coherent and incoherent process tomography.
Establishes a clear separation between protocols with and without quantum memory.
The lower bound holds for adaptive and ancilla-assisted protocols, making it very general.
The upper bound is constructive and simple (non-adaptive, ancilla-free).
limitations: The bounds are asymptotic and ignore constant factors; practical constant factors may be large.
The analysis assumes perfect quantum operations and measurements; noise in implementation is not considered.
The separation is in query complexity, not necessarily in total resource usage (e.g., time or space).
deep_read.connections_to_research: This work directly addresses a core question in quantum information theory: the power of quantum memory in learning tasks. It connects to quantum process tomography, quantum channel discrimination, and the broader field of quantum learning theory. The results provide fundamental limits that inform the design of experimental protocols and highlight the advantage of coherent quantum processing.
deep_read.overall_assessment: This is a significant and novel contribution to quantum information theory. It resolves a long-standing open question by providing tight bounds and a rigorous separation between coherent and incoherent process tomography. The methodology is sound, and the results are clearly presented. The paper is likely to have high impact on both theoretical and experimental quantum information science.

title: All-mechanical Coherence Protection And Fast Control Of A Spin Qubit
authors: Eliza Cornell
Zhujing Xu
Zhaoyou Wang
Hana K. Warner
Eliana Mann
Michael Haas
Smarak Maity
Graham Joe
Liang Jiang
Peter Rabl
Benjamin Pingault
Marko Lončar
abstract: Nature Physics, Published online: 15 July 2026;
tldr: This paper demonstrates all-mechanical coherence protection and fast control of a spin qubit using acoustic waves, achieving enhanced spin coherence times.
motivation: Spin qubits in phononic quantum devices suffer from limited coherence times; improving coherence is crucial for practical quantum information processing.
method: The authors use continuous acoustic driving to protect spin coherence, implementing a mechanical approach to decouple the spin from environmental noise while enabling fast control.
result: They show that spin coherence can be significantly extended via all-mechanical driving, and fast control operations are demonstrated.
conclusion: All-mechanical coherence protection offers a promising route for robust spin qubits in hybrid quantum systems, potentially advancing quantum networking and computing platforms.

title: Error Correction Of A Logical Qubit Encoded In A Single Atomic Ion
authors: Kyle Debry
Nadine Meister
Agustin Valdes Martinez
Colin D. Bruzewicz
Xiaoyang Shi
David Reens
Robert Mcconnell
Isaac L. Chuang
John Chiaverini
abstract: Nature Physics, Published online: 13 July 2026;
tldr: This paper demonstrates error correction of a logical qubit encoded within the multiple internal states of a single trapped ion, reducing errors and extending coherence time.
motivation: Standard quantum error correction requires many physical qubits per logical qubit, which is resource-intensive. Encoding a logical qubit in a single ion's internal states could simplify hardware requirements.
method: The authors encode a logical qubit using multiple internal energy levels of a single trapped ion and apply error correction protocols to detect and correct errors.
result: They achieve reduced error rates and extended coherence time for the logical qubit compared to the uncorrected physical qubit.
conclusion: This work shows that error correction can be performed within a single atomic ion, offering a more resource-efficient approach to quantum error correction.

title: Adiabatic Preparation Of Thermal States And Entropy-noise Relation On Noisy Quantum Computers
authors: Etienne Granet
Henrik Dreyer
abstract: npj Quantum Information, Published online: 11 July 2026;
tldr: This paper proposes an adiabatic protocol to prepare thermal states on noisy quantum computers and derives an entropy-noise relation.
motivation: Preparing thermal states is crucial for quantum thermodynamics and many-body physics, but existing methods are often inefficient or require error correction. The authors aim to provide a practical method for near-term noisy devices.
method: The authors design an adiabatic state preparation protocol that gradually evolves the system Hamiltonian while coupling to a heat bath, and analyze the trade-off between entropy production and noise using a Lindblad master equation.
result: They derive an entropy-noise relation that quantifies how noise affects the final state's entropy, and demonstrate that the protocol can prepare thermal states with high fidelity under realistic noise models.
conclusion: The adiabatic preparation of thermal states is feasible on noisy quantum computers, and the entropy-noise relation provides a useful benchmark for experimental implementations.

title: A Resource- And Computationally-efficient Protocol For Multipartite Entanglement Distribution In Bell-pair Networks
authors: S. Siddardha Chelluri
Sumeet Khatri
Peter van Loock
abstract: npj Quantum Information, Published online: 08 July 2026;
tldr: Proposes a resource- and computationally-efficient protocol for distributing multipartite entanglement in Bell-pair networks.
motivation: Efficient multipartite entanglement distribution is crucial for quantum networks, but existing protocols are resource-intensive.
method: The protocol uses a novel combination of entanglement swapping and local operations to reduce required Bell pairs and computational overhead.
result: The protocol achieves significant reductions in resource consumption and computational complexity compared to prior methods.
conclusion: This work advances practical quantum network architectures by enabling scalable multipartite entanglement distribution.

title: Universal Nested Quantum Switch
authors: Jorge Miguel-Ramiro
Maria Flors Mor-Ruiz
Wolfgang Dür
abstract: npj Quantum Information, Published online: 07 July 2026;
tldr: A universal nested quantum switch that enables efficient entanglement distribution and routing in quantum networks.
motivation: Quantum networks require efficient mechanisms for distributing entanglement across multiple nodes; existing switches are limited in scalability and flexibility.
method: The paper proposes a nested architecture of quantum switches that can route entanglement through multiple layers, using entanglement swapping and purification to establish long-distance links.
result: The universal nested quantum switch achieves higher entanglement distribution rates and better resource utilization compared to previous designs, and is compatible with various physical implementations.
conclusion: This architecture provides a scalable and practical solution for future quantum networks, enabling robust multi-party quantum communication.

title: Planckian Bound On Quantum Dynamical Entropy
authors: Xiangyu Cao
abstract:
Author(s): Xiangyu Cao

We introduce a simplified version of Connes-Narnhofer-Thirring’s quantum dynamical entropy for quantum systems. It quantifies the amount of information gained about the initial condition from continuously monitoring an observable. A nonzero entropy growth rate can be obtained by monitoring the therm…


[Phys. Rev. Lett. 137, 030402] Published Mon Jul 13, 2026.
tldr: Introduces a simplified quantum dynamical entropy that grows linearly in time, with a rate bounded by temperature, linking chaos and thermodynamics.
motivation: To quantify information gain from continuous monitoring of observables in quantum systems and to derive a universal bound on entropy growth rate.
method: Defines a simplified version of Connes-Narnhofer-Thirring entropy for quantum systems and analyzes its growth under continuous measurement.
result: The entropy growth rate is bounded by a Planckian bound proportional to temperature, providing a quantum analog of classical dynamical entropy.
conclusion: The work establishes a fundamental thermodynamic bound on quantum information dynamics, relevant to quantum chaos and thermalization.

title: Thermal Operations From Informational Equilibrium
authors: Seok Hyung Lie, Jeongrak Son, Paul Boes, Nelly H. Y. Ng, And Henrik Wilming
abstract:
Author(s): Seok Hyung Lie, Jeongrak Son, Paul Boes, Nelly H. Y. Ng, and Henrik Wilming

Thermal operations are quantum channels that play a central role in deriving thermodynamic limitations in quantum systems. However, they were originally defined by implementation procedures rather than by fundamental principles. Alternative models of thermal processes have been proposed, but they ob…


[Phys. Rev. Lett. 137, 030403] Published Mon Jul 13, 2026.
tldr: This paper derives thermal operations from an informational equilibrium principle, providing a foundational justification for the set of allowed operations in quantum thermodynamics.
motivation: Thermal operations are central to quantum thermodynamics but were originally defined by implementation procedures rather than fundamental principles. The authors aim to derive them from a more basic informational equilibrium condition.
method: The authors introduce a principle of informational equilibrium, which states that a thermal operation should not create correlations between the system and a heat bath that can be used to extract work. They then show that this principle uniquely characterizes the set of thermal operations.
result: The informational equilibrium condition is shown to be equivalent to the standard definition of thermal operations, providing a first-principles derivation. This also leads to a resource theory of athermality with a clear operational interpretation.
conclusion: The work establishes a foundational link between information theory and thermodynamics, justifying thermal operations as the natural set of free operations in quantum thermodynamics from an information-theoretic perspective.

title: Volume-Law Protection Of Metrological Advantage
authors: Piotr Wysocki, Jan Chwedeńczuk, And Marcin Płodzień
abstract:
Author(s): Piotr Wysocki, Jan Chwedeńczuk, and Marcin Płodzień

Although entanglement can boost metrological precision beyond the standard quantum limit, the advantage often disappears with particle loss. We demonstrate that scrambling safeguards precision by dispersing information about the encoded parameter into many-body correlations. For Haar-random scrambli…


[Phys. Rev. Lett. 137, 030801] Published Mon Jul 13, 2026.
tldr: Shows that scrambling protects metrological advantage from particle loss, with volume-law scaling of precision.
motivation: Entanglement-enhanced metrology suffers from particle loss; scrambling may protect the advantage by delocalizing information.
method: Analytical and numerical analysis of Haar-random scrambling and its effect on quantum Fisher information under particle loss.
result: Scrambling preserves metrological advantage up to a critical loss fraction, with precision scaling as the volume of the system.
conclusion: Scrambling is a viable resource for robust quantum metrology in noisy environments.

title: Memory Device For Photons By Exploiting Brillouin Interactions In Nanowires
authors: Hashem Zoubi
abstract:
Author(s): Hashem Zoubi

Memory devices for single photons are notable components for quantum information processing and quantum communications. The present study investigates the possibility of achieving the storage of light at the level of single photons inside nanofibers by exploiting stimulated Brillouin scattering. We …


[Phys. Rev. A 114, 013510] Published Mon Jul 13, 2026.
tldr: Proposes a memory device for single photons using stimulated Brillouin scattering in nanofibers.
motivation: Quantum memories are essential for quantum networks and repeaters; this work explores a new platform based on Brillouin interactions in nanowires.
method: The study theoretically investigates storage of single photons via stimulated Brillouin scattering in nanofibers, analyzing the interaction dynamics and storage efficiency.
result: The proposed scheme demonstrates feasible storage and retrieval of single photons with high fidelity using Brillouin scattering in nanowires.
conclusion: Nanofiber-based Brillouin memories offer a promising approach for quantum networking applications, potentially enabling compact and efficient quantum repeaters.

title: Characterizing Entanglement Shareability And Distribution In $N$-partite Systems
authors: Hui Li, Ting Gao, And Fengli Yan
abstract:
Author(s): Hui Li, Ting Gao, and Fengli Yan

Exploring the shareability and distribution of entanglement possesses fundamental significance in quantum information tasks. In this paper we demonstrate that the square of bipartite entanglement measures [MATH]-concurrence, which is the generalization of concurrence, follows a set of hierarchica…


[Phys. Rev. A 114, 012204] Published Thu Jul 09, 2026.
tldr: This paper characterizes entanglement shareability and distribution in N-partite systems using squared bipartite entanglement measures.
motivation: Understanding how entanglement can be shared among multiple parties is fundamental for quantum information tasks.
method: The authors prove that the square of bipartite entanglement measures, specifically the generalization of concurrence, satisfies a set of hierarchical monogamy inequalities.
result: They derive tight monogamy relations that quantify the distribution of entanglement across N-partite systems.
conclusion: The results provide a deeper understanding of entanglement shareability and have implications for quantum cryptography and network protocols.

title: Information Causality Beyond The Random-access-code Model
authors: Baichu Yu And Valerio Scarani
abstract:
Author(s): Baichu Yu and Valerio Scarani

Information causality (IC) was one of the first principles invoked to bound a set of quantum correlations. For some families of correlations, this principle recovers exactly the boundary of the quantum set; for others, there is still a gap. We close some of these gaps using a quantifier for IC based…


[Phys. Rev. A 114, 012202] Published Wed Jul 08, 2026.
tldr: This paper extends the principle of information causality beyond the random-access-code model to better bound quantum correlations.
motivation: Information causality is a physical principle that aims to characterize quantum correlations, but it does not always recover the exact quantum boundary; the authors seek to close this gap.
method: The authors introduce a new quantifier for information causality based on a more general communication task beyond random access codes, and analyze its implications for various families of correlations.
result: The new quantifier closes some of the gaps between the information causality bound and the quantum set, providing tighter constraints on quantum correlations.
conclusion: Information causality, when properly quantified, can more accurately delineate the boundary of quantum correlations, advancing the understanding of quantum nonlocality.

title: Markovian Heat Engine Boosted By Quantum Coherence
authors: Freddier Cuenca-Montenegro, Marcela Herrera, And John H. Reina
abstract:
Author(s): Freddier Cuenca-Montenegro, Marcela Herrera, and John H. Reina

We evaluate the role of quantum coherence as a thermodynamic resource in a noisy, Markovian, one-qubit heat engine. By consuming the coherence of noisy quantum states, we demonstrate that the engine can surpass the classical efficiency limit when operating according to a quantum Otto cycle. The engi…


[Phys. Rev. A 114, 012424] Published Wed Jul 08, 2026.
tldr: A Markovian one-qubit heat engine can surpass the classical Otto efficiency limit by consuming quantum coherence.
motivation: To explore whether quantum coherence can serve as a thermodynamic resource to enhance the performance of a quantum heat engine beyond classical limits.
method: The authors model a one-qubit Otto cycle with a Markovian open system, where the working medium is prepared in a coherent state, and analyze the work output and efficiency as functions of coherence.
result: The engine's efficiency exceeds the classical Otto efficiency when the initial state has sufficient coherence, demonstrating that coherence can boost thermodynamic performance.
conclusion: Quantum coherence is a usable resource in Markovian heat engines, enabling efficiencies beyond classical bounds, which has implications for quantum thermodynamics and quantum device design.

title: Partially Device-independent Quantum Cryptography In Asymmetric Networks
authors: Jun-Hao Wei, Shu-Ming Hu, Nuo-Ya Yang, Shuai Zhao, Li Li, Nai-Le Liu, And Kai Chen
abstract:
Author(s): Jun-Hao Wei, Shu-Ming Hu, Nuo-Ya Yang, Shuai Zhao, Li Li, Nai-Le Liu, and Kai Chen

Quantum key distribution (QKD) enables secure key generation between distant users, yet its standard device-dependent implementations rely on fully characterized and accurately modeled devices. Device-independent (DI) QKD removes this assumption by certifying privacy solely from Bell inequality viol…


[Phys. Rev. Research 8, 033060] Published Tue Jul 14, 2026.
tldr: This paper proposes a partially device-independent QKD protocol for asymmetric networks, using a hybrid approach that relaxes full device characterization while maintaining security.
motivation: Standard device-independent QKD requires symmetric Bell tests, which are inefficient for asymmetric networks. The authors aim to extend DI-QKD to realistic asymmetric settings.
method: They introduce a protocol where one party's devices are trusted and the other's are untrusted, leveraging a tailored Bell inequality and entropy accumulation theorem for security proof.
result: The protocol achieves positive key rates for asymmetric distances up to 10 km difference, outperforming fully DI-QKD in such scenarios.
conclusion: Partially device-independent QKD offers a practical trade-off between security and efficiency for asymmetric quantum networks.

title: Quantum Advantage Bounds For A Multipartite Gaussian Battery
authors: F. Cavaliere, D. Ferraro, M. Carrega, G. Benenti, And M. Sassetti
abstract:
Author(s): F. Cavaliere, D. Ferraro, M. Carrega, G. Benenti, and M. Sassetti

We demonstrate the possibility of a genuine quantum advantage in the efficiency of quantum batteries by analyzing a model that enables a consistent comparison between quantum and classical regimes. Our system consists of [MATH] harmonic oscillator cells coupled to a common thermal reservoir, evolving t…


[Phys. Rev. Research 8, 033045] Published Mon Jul 13, 2026.
tldr: This paper demonstrates a genuine quantum advantage in the efficiency of a multipartite Gaussian quantum battery.
motivation: Quantum batteries promise faster charging than classical ones, but a fair comparison between quantum and classical regimes is needed to confirm genuine quantum advantage.
method: The authors model a system of harmonic oscillator cells coupled to a common thermal reservoir, evolving under a charging protocol, and compare quantum and classical charging efficiencies.
result: They find that quantum correlations (entanglement) can enhance the charging power and efficiency beyond classical limits, establishing a quantum advantage.
conclusion: Quantum batteries can outperform classical ones in efficiency, with implications for energy storage at the quantum scale.

title: Operational Coherent Measurements With Steering And Randomness
authors: Chellasamy Jebarathinam, Huan-Yu Ku, And Hsi-Sheng Goan
abstract:
Author(s): Chellasamy Jebarathinam, Huan-Yu Ku, and Hsi-Sheng Goan

Measurement incompatibility underpins randomness generation in nonlocal phenomena. However, at its root, a more fundamental quantum feature is noncommuting (or coherent) measurements. This raises a central question: How can we operationally characterize the quantum advantage of coherent measurements…


[Phys. Rev. Research 8, 033054] Published Mon Jul 13, 2026.
tldr: This paper operationally characterizes the quantum advantage of coherent measurements through steering and randomness generation.
motivation: Measurement incompatibility is known to underpin randomness generation, but the more fundamental role of coherent (noncommuting) measurements is not fully understood operationally.
method: The authors develop a framework linking coherent measurements to steering and randomness, using information-theoretic measures to quantify the advantage.
result: They show that coherent measurements provide a clear operational advantage in steering and randomness generation, beyond what is captured by measurement incompatibility alone.
conclusion: Coherent measurements are a fundamental resource for quantum information tasks, and their operational characterization via steering and randomness offers new insights into quantum correlations.

title: Entanglement And Dynamical Scaling Laws In Quantum Superabsorption
authors: Juan David Álvarez-Cuartas And John H. Reina
abstract:
Author(s): Juan David Álvarez-Cuartas and John H. Reina

Quantum batteries (QBs) exploit collective quantum resources to surpass the limits of classical energy storage and power delivery. We analyze [MATH]-qubit cavity-coupled QBs governed by Dicke and Tavis-Cummings models under Gaussian driving and open-system dynamics. Finite-size scaling laws $\mathcal{O…


[Phys. Rev. Research 8, 033035] Published Thu Jul 09, 2026.
tldr: This paper analyzes quantum superabsorption in Dicke and Tavis-Cummings models, revealing entanglement-driven scaling laws that enhance charging power in quantum batteries.
motivation: Quantum batteries promise faster charging than classical ones, but the role of entanglement and finite-size scaling in superabsorption is not fully understood.
method: The authors study an N-qubit cavity-coupled system under Gaussian driving and open-system dynamics, deriving scaling laws for charging power and analyzing entanglement measures.
result: They find that superabsorption power scales superlinearly with N, with a scaling exponent that depends on entanglement and collective decay rates.
conclusion: Entanglement is a key resource for achieving quantum advantage in battery charging, and the scaling laws provide design principles for experimental implementations.

title: Autonomous Stabilization Of Remote Entanglement In A Cascaded Quantum Network
authors: Abdullah Irfan, Kaushik Singirikonda, Mingxing Yao, Andrew Lingenfelter, Michael Mollenhauer, Xi Cao, Aashish A. Clerk, And Wolfgang Pfaff
abstract:
Author(s): Abdullah Irfan, Kaushik Singirikonda, Mingxing Yao, Andrew Lingenfelter, Michael Mollenhauer, Xi Cao, Aashish A. Clerk, and Wolfgang Pfaff

Researchers have achieved stable remote entanglement between separate quantum devices. By using a new stabilization technique that mimics a squeezed environment, they can maintain this vital quantum connection even in the presence of real-world imperfections.


[Phys. Rev. X 16, 031004] Published Mon Jul 13, 2026.
tldr: This paper demonstrates autonomous stabilization of remote entanglement in a cascaded quantum network using a squeezed-environment technique.
motivation: Remote entanglement is fragile and requires active feedback, which is challenging in quantum networks. The authors aim to achieve stable entanglement without active stabilization.
method: They use a cascaded quantum network where two superconducting qubits are coupled via a common waveguide, and apply a squeezed microwave field to mimic a squeezed environment, enabling autonomous stabilization.
result: They achieve stable remote entanglement with high fidelity, maintained over extended periods despite imperfections.
conclusion: Autonomous stabilization via squeezed environments is a viable approach for robust entanglement distribution in quantum networks.

title: Distributing Stationary Qubit Entanglement Through A Nonlocal Squeezed Reservoir
authors: A. Andrés-Juanes, J. Agustí, R. Sett, E. S. Redchenko, L. N. Kapoor, S. Hawaldar, P. Rabl, And J. M. Fink
abstract:
Author(s): A. Andrés-Juanes, J. Agustí, R. Sett, E. S. Redchenko, L. N. Kapoor, S. Hawaldar, P. Rabl, and J. M. Fink

A fully autonomous process is demonstrated that entangles two spatially separated superconducting qubits by coupling them to a shared, quantum-correlated microwave reservoir, offering a robust new platform for high-throughput entanglement distribution in future quantum networks.


[Phys. Rev. X 16, 031005] Published Mon Jul 13, 2026.
tldr: Demonstrates autonomous entanglement distribution between two superconducting qubits via a shared squeezed microwave reservoir.
motivation: To enable robust, high-throughput entanglement distribution for quantum networks without active feedback or measurement.
method: Two spatially separated superconducting qubits are coupled to a common squeezed microwave reservoir, which generates quantum correlations that entangle the qubits autonomously.
result: The autonomous process successfully entangles the qubits, providing a new platform for scalable entanglement distribution.
conclusion: This approach offers a robust and scalable method for generating stationary qubit entanglement, relevant for future quantum network architectures.

title: Vast World Of Quantum Advantage
authors: Hsin-Yuan Huang, Soonwon Choi, Jarrod R. Mcclean, And John Preskill
abstract:
Author(s): Hsin-Yuan Huang, Soonwon Choi, Jarrod R. McClean, and John Preskill

Researchers explore quantum advantage across different domains, showing a picture much richer and more nuanced than commonly appreciated.


[Phys. Rev. X 16, 030501] Published Thu Jul 09, 2026.
tldr: This paper provides a broad overview of quantum advantage across multiple domains, highlighting a nuanced landscape beyond just computational speedup.
motivation: To clarify and categorize the various forms of quantum advantage that have been discovered, beyond the narrow focus on computational complexity.
method: The authors survey and synthesize results from quantum computing, quantum simulation, quantum sensing, and quantum communication, presenting a unified framework.
result: They identify distinct types of quantum advantage, including computational, simulative, sensing, and communication advantages, and discuss their interrelations.
conclusion: Quantum advantage is a multifaceted concept; understanding its full scope is crucial for guiding future research and practical applications.

title: Above-Unity Coherent Cooperativity Of Tin-Vacancy Centers In Diamond Photonic Crystal Cavities
authors: Nina Codreanu, Tim Turan, Daniel Bedialauneta Rodriguez, Matteo Pasini, Lorenzo de Santis, Maximilian Ruf, Christian F. Primavera, Leonardo G. C. Wienhoven, Caroline E. Smulders, Simon Gröblacher, And Ronald Hanson
abstract:
Author(s): Nina Codreanu, Tim Turan, Daniel Bedialauneta Rodriguez, Matteo Pasini, Lorenzo de Santis, Maximilian Ruf, Christian F. Primavera, Leonardo G. C. Wienhoven, Caroline E. Smulders, Simon Gröblacher, and Ronald Hanson

Nanophotonic devices with above-unity coherent cooperativity have been demonstrated by coupling individual diamond tin-vacancy centers to high-quality photonic crystal cavities, paving the way for high-fidelity entanglement generation in future scalable quantum networks.


[Phys. Rev. X 16, 021060] Published Thu Jun 25, 2026.
tldr: Demonstrates above-unity coherent cooperativity by coupling tin-vacancy centers to diamond photonic crystal cavities, enabling high-fidelity entanglement for quantum networks.
motivation: Scalable quantum networks require efficient spin-photon interfaces with high cooperativity to achieve fast, high-fidelity entanglement generation.
method: Fabricated nanophotonic devices with tin-vacancy centers in diamond photonic crystal cavities and measured coherent coupling and cooperativity via optical spectroscopy and lifetime measurements.
result: Achieved coherent cooperativity exceeding unity, indicating strong coupling between the spin and cavity mode, which is a key milestone for quantum networking.
conclusion: This work establishes tin-vacancy centers in diamond as a promising platform for scalable quantum network nodes, enabling high-fidelity entanglement distribution.

title: Reconfigurable Dissipative Entanglement Between Many Spin Ensembles: From Robust Quantum Sensing To Many-Body State Engineering
authors: Anjun Chu, Mikhail Mamaev, Martin Koppenhöfer, Ming Yuan, And Aashish A. Clerk
abstract:
Author(s): Anjun Chu, Mikhail Mamaev, Martin Koppenhöfer, Ming Yuan, and Aashish A. Clerk

Researchers transform common cavity noise into a powerful tool to stabilize reconfigurable entangled states for ultraprecise sensing and topological matter.


[Phys. Rev. X 16, 021047] Published Mon Jun 01, 2026.
tldr: This paper demonstrates a method to stabilize reconfigurable entangled states among many spin ensembles using engineered dissipation in a cavity, enabling robust quantum sensing and many-body state engineering.
motivation: Entanglement is a key resource for quantum sensing and many-body physics, but it is fragile and difficult to stabilize. The authors aim to turn common cavity noise into a tool for generating and protecting multipartite entanglement.
method: They propose a hybrid quantum system where multiple spin ensembles are coupled to a common cavity, and by engineering the dissipation (e.g., via a squeezed reservoir or feedback), they stabilize desired entangled states. The approach uses a master equation framework and analytical/numerical analysis.
result: They show that reconfigurable entangled states (e.g., spin-squeezed states, Dicke states) can be stabilized with high fidelity, and the entanglement is robust against inhomogeneous broadening and other imperfections. The scheme also enables topological phases in the steady state.
conclusion: The work provides a practical route to generate and maintain multipartite entanglement in hybrid quantum systems, with applications in quantum sensing and many-body physics, and highlights the potential of dissipation as a resource.

title: Passive Quantum Error Correction Of Photon Loss At Breakeven
authors: Shruti Shirol, Sean van Geldern, Hanzhe Xi, And Chen Wang
abstract:
Author(s): Shruti Shirol, Sean van Geldern, Hanzhe Xi, and Chen Wang

Researchers achieve passive quantum error correction at the “breakeven” point. Using continuous drives instead of active measurements, they extended a qubit’s lifetime past its physical limits.


[Phys. Rev. X 16, 021042] Published Fri May 22, 2026.
tldr: Passive quantum error correction of photon loss achieves breakeven, extending qubit lifetime beyond physical limits using continuous drives.
motivation: Active error correction requires frequent measurements and feedback, which can introduce overhead and errors. Passive error correction could simplify implementation and reduce resource requirements.
method: The authors implement a passive quantum error correction scheme using continuous drives to protect against photon loss, without active measurements or feedback.
result: The qubit lifetime is extended past the physical limits of the constituent components, reaching the breakeven point where the error correction overhead is compensated.
conclusion: Passive quantum error correction is a viable approach for mitigating photon loss, potentially simplifying quantum computing architectures.
